title: Magnetism & Matter
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Bar Magnet & Dipole Equivalence, Cutting a Magnet, Gauss's Law in Magnetism, Earth's Magnetic Elements (Declination, Dip, Apparent Dip), Magnetometers & Dia-, Para- and Ferromagnetic Materials
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: Why Do Permanent Magnets Exist if Magnetic Monopoles Do Not?

In Electrostatics (Chapter 15), positive ($+q$) and negative ($-q$) charges can be isolated independently. In Magnetism, however, if you saw a bar magnet in half to separate its North ($N$) and South ($S$) poles, you simply get two smaller complete magnets, each with its own North and South pole! Even at the subatomic scale, an isolated magnetic North or South pole (Magnetic Monopole) has never been found.

Why? Because all magnetism in matter originates from tiny atomic current loops—electrons orbiting nuclei and spinning on their axes! A permanent bar magnet is simply a block of iron in which trillions of microscopic atomic current loops ($\vec{\mu} = I\vec{A}$) are aligned in the same direction, making a bar magnet 100% mathematically equivalent to a current-carrying solenoid!

Exact Equivalence Between Electrostatics and Magnetostatics:
Every formula from Electric Dipoles (Chapter 15) converts directly into a Bar Magnet formula by replacing:
• Electric Field $\vec{E} \longrightarrow$ Magnetic Field $\vec{B}$
• Electric Dipole Moment $\vec{p} \longrightarrow$ Magnetic Dipole Moment $\vec{M}$ (or $\vec{\mu}$)
• Coulomb Constant $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \longrightarrow \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$
• Electric Charge $q \longrightarrow$ Pole Strength $q_m$ (or $m$, SI unit: $\text{A}\cdot\text{m}$).

topics.title: Bar Magnet as an Equivalent Solenoid, Pole Strength, Cutting & Bending a Magnet, Dipole Field & Angular SHM
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Pole Strength ($q_m$), Magnetic Moment ($\vec{M}$) & Cutting/Bending a Bar Magnet
Pole Strength ($q_m$) vs. Magnetic Dipole Moment ($\vec{M}$):
• Pole Strength ($q_m$): Depends purely on the cross-sectional area $A$ of the magnet ($q_m \propto A$; SI Unit: $\text{A}\cdot\text{m}$). Force on a pole in field $\vec{B}$ is $\vec{F} = \pm q_m \vec{B}$ ($+$ for North pole, $-$ for South pole).
• Magnetic Dipole Moment ($\vec{M}$): Directed strictly from South ($S$) pole to North ($N$) pole inside the magnet: $$\boxed{\vec{M} = q_m (2\vec{\ell})} \qquad \left(\text{SI Unit: } \text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2 = \text{J/T}\right)$$
Operation on Bar Magnet (Original $q_m$, Length $L$, Moment $M = q_m L$)New Pole Strength ($q_m'$)New Magnetic Length ($L'$)New Magnetic Moment ($M' = q_m' L'$)
1. Cut Longitudinal (Parallel to Axis) into $n$ equal strips$$q_m' = \frac{q_m}{n}$$$L' = L$$$\boxed{M' = \frac{M}{n}}$$
2. Cut Transverse (Perpendicular to Axis) into $n$ equal pieces$q_m' = q_m$ (Unchanged!)$$L' = \frac{L}{n}$$$$\boxed{M' = \frac{M}{n}}$$
3. Bent into a Circular Arc of Angle $\theta$ (in radians)
(Arc length $L = R\theta$, chord length $L' = 2R\sin(\theta/2)$)		$q_m' = q_m$$$L' = \frac{2L}{\theta}\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)$$$$\boxed{M' = \frac{2M}{\theta}\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}$$
(For Semicircle $\theta = \pi$: $\boxed{M' = \frac{2M}{\pi}}$)
1.2 Magnetic Field, Torque, Potential Energy & Oscillation Magnetometer
$$\text{1. Axial Field } (\theta = 0^\circ): \; \boxed{\vec{B}_{\text{axial}} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2\vec{M}}{r^3}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{2. Equatorial Field } (\theta = 90^\circ): \; \boxed{\vec{B}_{\text{eq}} = -\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{\vec{M}}{r^3}}$$
$$\text{3. Torque in Uniform } \vec{B}: \; \boxed{\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{4. Potential Energy:} \; \boxed{U(\theta) = -\vec{M}\cdot\vec{B} = -M B \cos\theta}$$
$$\textbf{5. Oscillation (Vibration) Magnetometer Time Period:} \qquad \boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{M B_H}}}$$

Where $I = \frac{1}{12}m(L^2 + b^2)$ is the rotational moment of inertia of the bar magnet about its suspension axis, and $B_H$ is the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field.
topics.derivationHtml:
Sum & Difference Method for Comparing Two Bar Magnets (M₁ and M₂) in a Vibration Magnetometer

When two bar magnets of moments $M_1, M_2$ and moments of inertia $I_1, I_2$ are tied together and suspended in $B_H$:

1. Like Poles Together (Sum Position, $M_s = M_1 + M_2$): $T_1 = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I_1 + I_2}{(M_1 + M_2)B_H}}$.

2. Unlike Poles Together (Difference Position, $M_d = M_1 - M_2$): $T_2 = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I_1 + I_2}{(M_1 - M_2)B_H}}$.

Squaring and dividing gives the high-speed JEE comparison formula:

$$\frac{T_2^2}{T_1^2} = \frac{M_1 + M_2}{M_1 - M_2} \implies \boxed{\frac{M_1}{M_2} = \frac{T_2^2 + T_1^2}{T_2^2 - T_1^2}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap (How Time Period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{MB_H}}$ Changes When a Bar Magnet of Length $L$ Is Cut Transversely into $n$ Equal Pieces!):
    When cut perpendicular to its length into $n$ equal pieces:
    • Mass becomes $m' = \frac{m}{n}$ and length becomes $L' = \frac{L}{n}$, so moment of inertia drops by $n^3$: $\mathbf{I' = \frac{1}{12}\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)\left(\frac{L}{n}\right)^2 = \frac{I}{n^3}}$!
    • Magnetic moment drops by $n$: $\mathbf{M' = \frac{M}{n}}$.
    • Therefore, the new time period of one small piece is $\boxed{T' = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I/n^3}{(M/n)B_H}} = \frac{T}{n}}$! (Whereas if cut longitudinally into $n$ strips, both $I' = I/n$ and $M' = M/n$, so $T' = T$ remains unchanged!).

topics.title: Gauss's Law in Magnetism, Earth's Magnetic Elements (Declination, Angle of Dip, Apparent Dip) & Tangent Galvanometer
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Gauss's Law for Magnetism ($\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0$)
Statement & Physical Meaning:
The net magnetic flux through ANY closed 3D surface is always identically zero:
$$\boxed{\Phi_B = \oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0}$$

Why? Because magnetic monopoles do not exist! Every magnetic field line is a continuous closed loop (from $N \to S$ outside the magnet and from $S \to N$ inside the magnet), so every line that enters a closed surface must also exit it.

2.2 The 3 Elements of Earth's Magnetic Field ($\theta$, $\delta$, $B_H$)
  • 1. Magnetic Declination ($\theta$): The acute angle between the Geographic Meridian (vertical plane passing through geographic North-South axis) and the Magnetic Meridian (vertical plane in which a freely suspended compass needle aligns).
  • 2. Angle of Dip / Inclination ($\delta$): The angle that Earth's net magnetic field vector $\vec{B}_e$ (in the magnetic meridian) makes with the horizontal:
    $$\boxed{B_H = B_e \cos\delta, \qquad B_V = B_e \sin\delta} \implies \boxed{\tan\delta = \frac{B_V}{B_H}} \quad \text{and} \quad \boxed{B_e = \sqrt{B_H^2 + B_V^2}}$$
    • At Magnetic Equator: Field lines are purely horizontal ($B_V = 0, B_H = B_e$) $\implies \boxed{\delta = 0^\circ}$.
    • At Magnetic Poles: Field lines are purely vertical ($B_H = 0, B_V = B_e$) $\implies \boxed{\delta = 90^\circ}$.
  • 3. Apparent Angle of Dip ($\delta'$) in a Plane Rotated by Angle $\alpha$ from the Magnetic Meridian:
    When a dip circle is rotated by horizontal angle $\alpha$ away from the magnetic meridian, the vertical component $B_V$ stays unchanged, while the effective horizontal component in that plane shrinks to $B_H' = B_H\cos\alpha$:
    $$\boxed{\tan\delta' = \frac{B_V}{B_H\cos\alpha} = \frac{\tan\delta}{\cos\alpha}} \qquad \left(\text{Since } \cos\alpha < 1, \text{ apparent dip is ALWAYS greater than true dip: } \delta' > \delta\right)$$
    If apparent dips $\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$ are measured in two mutually perpendicular vertical planes ($\alpha$ and $90^\circ - \alpha$, so $\cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\alpha = 1$):
    $$\boxed{\cot^2\delta = \cot^2\delta_1 + \cot^2\delta_2}$$
2.3 Tangent Law of Perpendicular Fields ($B = B_H\tan\theta$)

When a compass needle is simultaneously subjected to Earth's horizontal field $B_H$ and a perpendicular horizontal magnetic field $B$ (e.g., at the center of a Tangent Galvanometer coil aligned in the magnetic meridian), the needle comes to rest at deflection angle $\theta$ with $B_H$ such that:

$$\boxed{B = B_H \tan\theta} \implies \text{Tangent Galvanometer:} \quad \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R} = B_H\tan\theta \implies \boxed{I = K\tan\theta} \quad \left(K = \frac{2 R B_H}{\mu_0 N}\right)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof of Orthogonal Planes Dip Relation: cot²δ = cot²δ₁ + cot²δ₂

In plane 1 (at angle $\alpha$ to magnetic meridian): $\tan\delta_1 = \frac{\tan\delta}{\cos\alpha} \implies \cos\alpha = \frac{\tan\delta}{\tan\delta_1} = \tan\delta\cot\delta_1$.

In plane 2 (at angle $90^\circ - \alpha$ to magnetic meridian): $\tan\delta_2 = \frac{\tan\delta}{\cos(90^\circ - \alpha)} = \frac{\tan\delta}{\sin\alpha} \implies \sin\alpha = \tan\delta\cot\delta_2$.

Squaring and adding ($\cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\alpha = 1$):

$$\tan^2\delta\left(\cot^2\delta_1 + \cot^2\delta_2\right) = 1 \implies \boxed{\cot^2\delta = \cot^2\delta_1 + \cot^2\delta_2}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap (Compass Needle vs. Dip Circle Needle at the Magnetic Poles): At the magnetic poles ($\delta = 90^\circ$), $B_H = 0$ and $B_V = B_e$:
    • A horizontal compass needle (constrained to rotate only in the horizontal plane) experiences zero horizontal restoring torque ($B_H = 0$), so it can point in ANY arbitrary horizontal direction!
    • A dip circle needle (free to rotate in the vertical plane) aligns strictly vertical ($90^\circ$)!

topics.title: Magnetizing Field (H), Magnetization (I/M), Susceptibility (χ), Permeability (μr), Dia/Para/Ferromagnetism, Curie's Law & Hysteresis
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 The 4 Fundamental Magnetic Material Vectors & Constants ($\vec{H}, \vec{I}, \chi_m, \mu_r$)

Suppose a solenoid with air core creates a magnetizing field $\vec{H}$ ($B_0 = \mu_0 H$, where $H = n I$ has SI unit $\text{A/m}$). When a material core is inserted inside the solenoid, atomic dipoles align and produce an additional internal magnetic field $\mu_0 \vec{I}$:

$$\text{1. Intensity of Magnetization (Magnetic Moment per Unit Volume):} \qquad \boxed{\vec{I}_{\text{mag}} = \frac{\vec{M}_{\text{net}}}{V}} \qquad (\text{SI Unit: } \text{A/m, same as } H!)$$
$$\text{2. Magnetic Susceptibility:} \quad \boxed{\chi_m = \frac{I_{\text{mag}}}{H}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{3. Total Field Inside Core:} \quad \boxed{\vec{B} = \mu_0(\vec{H} + \vec{I}_{\text{mag}}) = \mu_0(1 + \chi_m)\vec{H} = \mu_0 \mu_r \vec{H} = \mu \vec{H}}$$
$$\textbf{Master Link Between Relative Permeability } (\mu_r) \textbf{ and Susceptibility } (\chi_m): \qquad \boxed{\mu_r = \frac{\mu}{\mu_0} = 1 + \chi_m}$$
3.2 Complete Comparison: Diamagnetic vs. Paramagnetic vs. Ferromagnetic Materials

$\boxed{\chi_m = \frac{C}{T - T_c}}$ (becomes Paramagnetic above Curie temp $T_c$!)
3.3 Hysteresis Loop ($B$-$H$ Curve): Soft Iron vs. Steel
  • Retentivity (Remanence $OB$): Residual magnetization ($B$) remaining in the material when the magnetizing field $H$ is reduced back to zero.
  • Coercivity ($OC$): Reverse magnetizing field ($-H$) required to completely demagnetize the material ($B = 0$).
  • Area of the $B$-$H$ Hysteresis Loop: Equals the thermal energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle of magnetization!
    • Soft Iron (Used for Transformer Cores & Electromagnets): High permeability, high retentivity, LOW coercivity, and NARROW hysteresis loop (minimum energy loss!).
    • Hard Steel / Alnico (Used for Permanent Magnets): High retentivity and VERY HIGH coercivity (wide hysteresis loop so external stray fields cannot easily demagnetize it!).
topics.derivationHtml:
Meissner Effect in Superconductors (Perfect Diamagnetism: B = 0, χ_m = −1, μ_r = 0)

When a superconductor is cooled below its critical temperature $T_c$, it expels all magnetic flux from its interior ($\vec{B}_{\text{inside}} = 0$, called the Meissner Effect). Substituting $B = 0$ into $B = \mu_0(1 + \chi_m)H = \mu_0 \mu_r H$ gives:

$$\boxed{\mu_r = 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \chi_m = -1} \qquad (\text{Perfect Diamagnet!})$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Diamagnetism Is Present in ALL Materials!): Because Lenz's law orbital induction acts on paired electrons in every atom, diamagnetism is universal—however, in paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials, it is masked by the much stronger positive alignment of unpaired electron spins. That is also why diamagnetic susceptibility $\chi_m$ is completely independent of temperature $T$!
  • Trap 2 (Liquid in a U-Tube Placed Between Magnetic Poles): If a paramagnetic liquid is placed in a U-tube with one limb between strong magnetic poles, the liquid rises in the limb between the poles (attracted to strong field); if the liquid is diamagnetic (like water), its level falls/depresses between the poles!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 19: Magnetism & Matter! Next, in Chapter 20, we discover how changing magnetic flux creates electric fields and induced currents in Electromagnetic Induction.
summary:
• Bar Magnet: $\vec{M} = q_m(2\vec{\ell})$; Bent into arc $\theta$: $M' = \frac{2M}{\theta}\sin(\theta/2)$; Vibration magnetometer $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{MB_H}}$.
  • Earth's Magnetism: $B_H = B_e\cos\delta$, $B_V = B_e\sin\delta$, $\tan\delta = \frac{B_V}{B_H}$; Apparent dip $\tan\delta' = \frac{\tan\delta}{\cos\alpha}$ and $\cot^2\delta = \cot^2\delta_1 + \cot^2\delta_2$.
  • Magnetic Materials: $\vec{B} = \mu_0(\vec{H} + \vec{I})$, $\chi_m = \frac{I}{H}$, $\mu_r = 1 + \chi_m$.
  • Dia / Para / Ferro: Dia ($\chi_m < 0$, $T$-independent); Para ($\chi_m = C/T > 0$); Ferro ($\chi_m \gg 1$, becomes para above $T_c$).

questions.prompt: A thin bar magnet of magnetic dipole moment $M$ is bent at its midpoint so that its two equal halves make an angle of $60^\circ$ with each other. What is the new magnetic dipole moment $M'$ of the bent magnet?
questions.explanation: When bent at the midpoint (each half has length $L/2$) at $60^\circ$, the two halves and the line joining the poles form an equilateral triangle of side $L/2$! Thus the new separation between the South and North poles is $L' = \frac{L}{2}$, giving $M' = q_m L' = \frac{M}{2}$.

questions.prompt: At a certain location on Earth, the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field is $B_H = \sqrt{3}\,B_V$ (where $B_V$ is the vertical component). What is the angle of dip $\delta$ at this location?

A thin bar magnet of length $L$ and magnetic moment $M$ has a time period $T$ in a vibration magnetometer. If the magnet is cut perpendicular to its length into 3 equal pieces, what will be the time period of oscillation of any ONE of the three pieces in the same magnetic field?
questions.explanation: When cut transversely into $n = 3$ equal pieces, mass becomes $m/3$ and length becomes $L/3$, so moment of inertia becomes $I' = \frac{I}{3^3} = \frac{I}{27}$, while magnetic moment becomes $M' = \frac{M}{3}$. Thus $T' = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I/27}{(M/3)B_H}} = \frac{T}{\sqrt{9}} = \frac{T}{3}$.

questions.prompt: If a dip circle is placed in a vertical plane at an angle of $\alpha = 60^\circ$ to the magnetic meridian, the dip needle makes an angle of $\delta' = 45^\circ$ with the horizontal. What is the true angle of dip $\delta$ at that place?

A paramagnetic sample shows a net magnetization of $8\text{ A/m}$ when placed in an external magnetic field of $0.6\text{ T}$ at a temperature of $4\text{ K}$. When the same sample is placed in an external magnetic field of $0.2\text{ T}$ at a temperature of $16\text{ K}$, what will be its magnetization?
questions.explanation: By Curie's Law for a paramagnetic material, $I_{\text{mag}} = \chi H \propto \frac{B}{T}$. Therefore, $\frac{I_2}{I_1} = \left(\frac{B_2}{B_1}\right)\left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right) = \left(\frac{0.2}{0.6}\right)\left(\frac{4}{16}\right) = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{12} \implies I_2 = \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}\text{ A/m}$.

questions.prompt: A solenoid has $n = 1000\text{ turns/m}$ and carries a current of $I = 2\text{ A}$. Its core is filled with iron having relative permeability $\mu_r = 500$. Find (i) the magnetizing field $H$, and (ii) the intensity of magnetization $I_{\text{mag}}$ of the iron core.
questions.explanation: (i) Magnetizing field $H = nI = 1000 \times 2 = 2000\text{ A/m}$. (ii) Since $\chi_m = \mu_r - 1 = 500 - 1 = 499$, the intensity of magnetization is $I_{\text{mag}} = \chi_m H = 499 \times 2000 = 9.98 \times 10^5\text{ A/m}$.
